approachQuestion.prompt:
Closest inspection periods

Two laboratories provide closed operating periods A and B, each list sorted by start and internally strictly separated: end[i] < start[i+1]. Return the smallest distance between any point in an A period and any point in a B period. The distance is 0 when any periods intersect, including at one endpoint. Inputs are immutable; return one integer.

Input: A=[[1,3],[10,12]], B=[[5,8],[15,16]]
Output: 2
The gaps from 3 to 5 and from 8 to 10 both have length 2.

Input: A=[[2,5]], B=[[5,7]]
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ m,n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ start ≤ end ≤ 1000000000. Both inputs support indexed reads. Choose best worst-case time, then least auxiliary memory.

options.text: Compare current A and B periods. Return 0 if they intersect. Otherwise update the minimum endpoint gap, then advance the period with the smaller end. Continue until one list ends.
options.feedback: For disjoint current periods, the earlier one cannot get closer to any later period of the other list than the gap just checked. If they intersect, no distance can beat zero.

options.text: Compare only A[i] with B[i] for every index present in both arrays, returning the smallest distance.
options.feedback: For A=[[0,1],[100,101]] and B=[[10,11],[20,21],[102,103]], this misses the distance 1 between the last A period and the last B period.

options.text: Find the minimum absolute difference between start coordinates from A and B.
options.feedback: For A=[[1,10]] and B=[[8,9]], the periods intersect and distance is 0, while the starts differ by 7. Width and endpoints matter.

options.text: Compute the distance for every A,B period pair and take the minimum.
options.feedback: This is correct, but checks all pairs even though order proves which earlier period can be discarded after each comparison.

feedback.reason: Translate interval separation into a minimum-distance objective and safely discard the earlier frontier.
details: Use two forward indices and one current best gap. Compare current endpoints, return immediately on intersection, or update the gap and advance the earlier-ending period. Use no copies, temporary lists or recursion.

Overlapping periods give zero gap immediately. Otherwise the earlier-ending period cannot be closer to a future, later period than the current comparison, so advance it. Sorted disjoint lists make this elimination safe.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For distance-two-frontiers, analyze worst-case total time in nonempty list lengths m,n and auxiliary space. An early return may improve particular inputs; choose the tightest worst-case pair.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

feedback.reason: Each unsuccessful comparison advances at least one period index.
details: Each unsuccessful comparison advances at least one index, so at most m+n such steps occur. Interleaved but disjoint periods can force a linear number of steps. The best gap, endpoints and two indices are constant auxiliary state; neither input is copied.
Worst case for the specified iterative two-frontier scan; scalar result.
“Time O(mn), auxiliary space O(1)”: No independent all-pairs loop is used. Each unsuccessful comparison advances a forward index.
“Time O(m+n), auxiliary space O(m+n)”: The input lists are read directly; there is no temporary list or copy. The maintained gap and indices are constant state.
“Time O(log(m+n)), auxiliary space O(1)”: This method does not binary-search a shared monotone coordinate space. Interleaved periods may require a linear number of index advances.
